title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 14 (19/08/2019)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 19 AUGUST 2019
Subject: The Respondent challenged one of the Arbitrators (nominated by the Parties
from a list provided by the LCIA) pursuant to Article 10.3 of the LCIA Rules
2014.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: New York, United States of America
Governing Law of New York law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to the Arbitrator’s relationship with the Claimant’s
quantum expert, who was simultaneously acting as an expert upon instruction
of the Arbitrator’s law firm in an unrelated arbitration in which the Arbitrator
was the lead counsel.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
The arbitration being organised under the LCIA Rules, it is justified and
required, when determining whether “justifiable doubts” as envisaged by
Article 10.1 of the LCIA Rules exist, to take into account what the LCIA Court
has held in other cases where the term had to be applied. However, the
relevance of the determinations made in other LCIA References may be
limited by the arbitration law which was applicable in those cases and which
may have influenced the determination. Therefore, US law authorities will also
be taken into account as the term “justifiable doubts” has to be interpreted
also in accordance with the applicable arbitration law.
The circumstances of the present challenge have to be assessed “reasonably”,
that is, through the eyes of a reasonable third person, under US law, and this
standard aligns well with the LCIA standard.
Contemporaneous parallel contacts of an arbitrator with one of the Parties’
experts may give rise to doubts which are reasonable and even the prospect
of such contacts is sufficient to justly alert the other party. However, in
circumstances where the Arbitrator did not choose or engage the expert in
the unrelated arbitration (another partner at the law firm did), had not
substantially worked with the expert, and the subject matter of the expert’s
reports in both cases is different, the Arbitrator’s impartiality or independence
are not impaired.
One single meeting (shortly after the expert’s appointment and four months
before his report in the unrelated arbitration was due) and a few telephone

calls “are clearly not of the kind and number which would normally be required
to create between two professionals a relationship of dependency or entailing
partiality.”
If the relationship were to continue, and if the expert and the Arbitrator
(whether or not as member of the larger team at the firm working in the
unrelated arbitration) were to work together more or less closely in a period
more or less concomitant with the hearing in the present arbitration, the
situation would be different. The concern that the Arbitrator “could not
impartially evaluate the testimony of an expert that the Arbitrator would be
vouching for in another matter” would in that scenario be understandable.
The Arbitrator’s statement, when disclosing the relationship with the expert,
that this was done out of an abundance of caution, did not impair impartiality
or independence, and was not improper. The Arbitrator was “perfectly
entitled” to say so if the Arbitrator considered that to be the case, and if not,
the Arbitrator would have had to resign.
The Arbitrator’s initial indication of willingness to withdraw, and the
subsequent refusal to do so in light of the Parties' submissions regarding the
potential replacement of the expert, which in the Arbitrator’s view no longer
required or justified withdrawal, was not improper and does not impair
independence or impartiality.
Decision 14 - 2

LCIA COURT OF INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION
Arbitration N° […]
[…]
CLAIMANT and COUNTERRESPONDENT
v
[…]
RESPONDENT and COUNTERCLAIMANT
Decision on Challenge of [Arbitrator A]
__________________________________________________________________________________
I. BACKGROUND AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
1. This challenge was brought in an arbitration between […] a company incorporated in the
United Kingdom, represented by [Law Firm A] (“Claimant”) and [...] a company incorporated in
the United States, represented by [Law Firm B], [Law Firm C], and [Law Firm D] (and previously
also by [Law Firm E]) (“Respondent” […] and, together with the Claimant, “the Parties”). The
arbitration arose from a “[…] Supply Agreement” dated 6 February 2012 (“the Agreement”)
between the Parties.
2. The Tribunal comprising [Arbitrator B], [Arbitrator A] and [Arbitrator C] was appointed by the
LCIA Court on 27 June 2018.
3. On 10 June 2019, [the Claimant] filed an expert report on damages by [Expert A], of [Company
X] […]. This prompted [Arbitrator A] on 13 June 2019 to make a disclosure as follows:
“I wish to disclose that my firm has retained [Expert A] as an expert in an
[institutional] arbitration in which I am lead counsel. […] We […] expect [Expert A]
will offer testimony on [licensing] and antitrust issues, but not damages. I have met
Decision 14 - 3

with [Expert A] once, and spoken to him on the phone a couple of times, but he is
largely working with other members of the team.
I do not believe these circumstances impair my impartiality or independence, but
disclose them out of an abundance of caution”.
4. On 19 June 2019, the Respondent emailed the Tribunal that
“the disclosure places [the Respondent] in an extremely awkward position.
….from [the Respondent’s] position the conflict is very real, involving the prospect of
[the Claimant’s] expert having parallel and contemporaneous ex parte contact with
one of the arbitrators, who then would be called upon to judge the qualifications and
credibility of that same expert at the hearing. Indeed, given the timing of [Expert A’s]
engagement, it appears that he would be preparing his report for [Arbitrator A] and
his partners at the same time that our hearing is underway.
We appreciate that resolution of this problem will likely impact everyone involved in
the arbitration, and we are prepared to cooperate fully to address the consequences
of this unfortunate situation. But we do not believe that [the Respondent] should be
required simply to waive the conflict and agree that one of the panel, no matter how
well intentioned, could have a contemporaneous relationship with its opponent’s
expert.”
5. On the same day, the Claimant confirmed that “prior to receiving [Arbitrator A’s] email, [Law
Firm A] and [the Claimant] were unaware of the involvement of [Expert A] and [Company X] in
the matter identified by [Arbitrator A]” as had reportedly also been stated by the Claimant’s
counsel during a telephone conversation with Respondent’s counsel which apparently took
place before the Respondent sent its letter of 19 June 2019. There is no indication in the file
that the Respondent has contested this statement of the Claimant.
6. At the Parties’ suggestion, the Tribunal held a telephone call with the Parties, on 25 June 2019,
during which the presiding arbitrator mentioned as a possibility that another partner from
[Company X] be engaged as a substitute for [Expert A].
7. On 26 June 2019, the Respondent followed up on the Tribunal’s suggestion by proposing a
“compromise” to the Claimant which would “obviate the need for a formal objection” to
[Expert A] and “minimize the duplication of work carried out by [Company X]”: [the
Respondent] was prepared to agree that another expert from [Company X] replace [Expert A]
as [the Claimant’s] expert “provided that the new expert and those assisting him or her in
formulating opinions are walled off from [Expert A] and the members of his team who
participated in the formulation of his opinions”, requiring “that the replacement expert and
his/her team not access the [Expert A] report”. The Respondent added that the September
2019 hearing dates would need to be re-set and that its team was not available during the
October dates proposed during the call.
Decision 14 - 4

8. Further email exchanges between the Parties of 26 June 2019 show that the Claimant made a
counterproposal consisting in [the Claimant’s] agreement to replace [Expert A], but only
provided that new expert can “review any and all work product generated today by [Expert A’s]
team and provided he or she can be supported by any other [Company X] employees except
those with whom [Expert A] has had or will have contact”; the Respondent did not accept this
counterproposal; that both Parties were aware of the next day being the last one for [the
Respondent] to bring a formal challenge to [Arbitrator A]; and that the Claimant refused to
agree to an extension of that deadline.
9. On 27 June 2019, the Respondent informed the Claimant that it had during the call with the
Tribunal of 25 June 2019, “indicated that disqualification should extend to the firm” of
[Company X] and announced that it would proceed to file the notice of challenge on that same
day. The Respondent filed the challenge later that day and sent also a copy of the challenge to
the Tribunal, requesting that the date for submission of its brief (8 July 2019) be suspended
until the resolution of the challenge.
10. On 28 June 2019, the LCIA acknowledged receipt of the Respondent’s Notice of Challenge
dated 27 June 2019 and invited the Claimant to comment on the Respondent’s statement that
it prefers to withdraw the challenge if the Claimant obtains a replacement expert. In its reply
email to the LCIA of 28 June 2019, the Claimant referred to its letter of the same day to both
the Tribunal and the Respondent in which it denounced the Respondent’s failure to mention
in its challenge notice the counterproposal made by the Claimant on 26 June 2019, reiterated
its position concerning [Expert A’s] replacement and concerning the lack of justification for an
“ethical wall” between the replacement expert and [Expert A’s] report and team, and opposed
a stay of the arbitration. Still on 28 June 2019, the Respondent sent an email to the Tribunal
indicating that he would not react to the Claimant’s letter of 28 June 2019 unless the Tribunal
requested it to do so.
11. On 29 June 2019, [Arbitrator A], having received not only a copy of the Notice of Challenge but
also of the correspondence exchanged between the Parties on 28 June 2019, wrote to the
Parties as follows:
“During the conference on Tuesday, I advised the parties that, if [the Respondent]
maintained its concerns about my continued participation as arbitrator in view of the fact
that [the Claimant] was using [Expert A] as an expert and my disclosure of [Expert A’s] role
as an expert in a matter I am handling as counsel, I would withdraw as arbitrator.
I have reviewed [the Claimant’s] and [the Respondent’s] submissions of this week, and I
now advise that if [the Claimant] proceeds as it now proposes, with a new expert from
[Company X] but without the ethical screens that [the Respondent] proposes, I would not
Decision 14 - 5

so withdraw (unless directed by the LCIA Court in response to any continued challenge by
[the Respondent]).”
12. On 1 July 2019, the Respondent wrote to the Tribunal “to clarify [the Respondent’s] pending
Challenge to [Arbitrator A]”. The Respondent referred to [Arbitrator A’s] communication of 29
June 2019 as “in effect embracing [the Claimant’s] position that a colleague of [Expert A] could
replace him without an ethical wall” and “underscor[ing] the original conflict of interest”. The
Respondent acknowledged that the only person who could have recognized the conflict was
[Expert A] “since presumably [Arbitrator A] did not know [the Claimant] had engaged [Expert
A] until his report was submitted, and [the Claimant] did not know that [Arbitrator A’s] team
had retained [Expert A] until [Arbitrator A] so advised the […] the Parties”. It also stated that
“the way in which this conflict has been handled by [Arbitrator A] demonstrates that “justifiable
doubts” exist about his impartiality and independence in this matter” and that “institutional
disqualification is appropriate to remove doubts about concurrent conflicting interests”.
13. The Claimant filed on 3 July 2019 its Opposition to [the Respondent’s] Challenge to Continued
Participation of [Arbitrator A].
14. In the meantime, on 30 June 2019, the Tribunal had informed the Parties that it was inclined
to proceed with the preparations for the hearing as scheduled in September in accordance
with [the Claimant’s] proposal to submit a new expert report whether or not [the Respondent]
proceeded with its challenge and had invited the Parties to confer about a schedule for the
filing of such new expert report and of the Parties’ respective pre-hearing briefs. A joint
schedule for these submissions was proposed by the Parties on 2 July and accepted by the
Tribunal on 5 July 2019. It provided for the filing of:
- [The Respondent’s] Pre-Hearing Arbitration Brief, on all issues other than damages, on 8
July 2019
- [The Claimant’s] new expert report on damages, on 31 July 2019
- [The Claimant’s] Pre-Hearing Arbitration Brief, on all issues other than damages, on 2
August 2019
- [The Respondent’s] Pre-Hearing Arbitration Brief on damages, on 9 August 2019
- Objections to the authenticity of exhibits, on 12 August 2019
- [The Claimant’s] Pre-Hearing Arbitration Brief on damages, on 19 August 2019
and for a pre-hearing conference on 21 August 2019 and the Hearing on 4 – 13 September
2019.
15. On 5 July 2019, the LCIA informed the parties and the Tribunal that, subject to prompt
comments from the Parties or [Arbitrator A], the challenge would be referred to the LCIA Court
pursuant to Article 10.6 of the Rules.
Decision 14 - 6

16. On 6 July 2019, [Arbitrator A] submitted his comments to the challenge, explaining his
successive positions on withdrawing voluntarily as he had expressed them in his disclosure of
13 June 2019, during the telephone call of the tribunal with the Parties on 25 June 2019, and,
lastly, in his email of 29 June 2019.
17. On 16 July 2019, the LCIA informed the Parties and the Tribunal that the Court had appointed
the undersigned […] to determine the challenge. The Parties also received a copy of her CV and
of the signed statement of independence and consent to appointment. No objections were
formulated.
18. On 25 July, the undersigned invited the Parties to inform her by 29 July 2019 of any further
comments they might have and to file their cost submissions by 30 July 2019 if possible.
19. By a letter dated 28 July 2019 and received by email on 29 July 2019, the Claimant reported
that it had begun to implement its counter-proposal, engaging a new expert on damages issues
from [Company X], and that the new expert report would be submitted on 31 July 2019 in
accordance with the schedule proposed by the Parties and directed by the Tribunal. Also on 29
July 2019, the Respondent filed its Supplemental Brief dated 28 July 2019 in support of its
challenge.
20. On 30 July 2019, the Claimant wrote regarding [the Claimant’s] legal costs incurred in relation
to [the Respondent’s] challenge.
II. THE RESPONDENT’S GROUNDS FOR CHALLENGE
21. According to the Respondent, [Arbitrator A] cannot continue to participate as an arbitrator
because of his relationship with [Expert A] who submitted in this arbitration a report on
damages as the Claimant’s expert. That relationship follows from [Expert A’s] simultaneously
acting as an expert upon instruction of [Arbitrator A’s] firm in an [institutional] arbitration in
which [Arbitrator A] is the lead counsel.
22. The Notice of Challenge quoted extensively from the Respondent’s email of 19 June 2019
which detailed its perspective of the conflict as a real one given “the prospect of [the
Claimant’s] expert having parallel and contemporaneous ex parte contact with one of the
arbitrators, who then would be called upon to judge the qualifications and credibility of that
same expert at the hearing”.
23. The Notice also stated that the Respondent had hoped that the Parties together with the
Tribunal could resolve the matter but, for lack of a timely resolution it had to file the challenge
in order to respect the 14 day period after becoming aware of the possible challenge ground.
Decision 14 - 7

24. The Notice further quoted from U.S. court decisions which concluded that where a party hired
new counsel who created a conflict because the arbitrator’s firm used the new counsel’s firm
for unrelated work, the appropriate remedy was to disqualify the firm that created the conflict,
not the arbitrator (Matter of Shomrock v. Fuks). The Respondent considered that its proposal
that [Expert A] be replaced with another expert from [Company X], provided that the latter
and his assistants for this report be walled off from [Expert A] and his team members who
assisted him for the report, would allow [Arbitrator A] to continue to serve on the Tribunal.
25. The Notice concluded that the Respondent would greatly prefer a replacement of the expert
but, if by someone from [Company X], with an ethical wall that guarantees independence of
the replacement expert’s work, to maintaining its challenge.
26. Over time, the Respondent has added further arguments. In its 1 July 2019 email to the Court
and the Tribunal, the Respondent objected to [Arbitrator A] having expressed in his disclosure
of 13 June 2019 the belief that the disclosed circumstances did not impair his independence or
impartiality and his individual view “prematurely” before the Parties or the Tribunal had the
opportunity to assess the conflict. The Respondent also objected to [Arbitrator A’s] email of 29
June 2019 (seen para. 11 above), according to which [Arbitrator A] was first ready to resign if
he would be challenged but was no longer prepared to do so when he learned that [the
Respondent] insisted on an ethical wall between [Expert A] and his substitute. According to the
Respondent, the way in which [Arbitrator A] has handled this conflict demonstrates that
justifiable doubts exist about his independence and impartiality. Consequently, the
Respondent confirmed its challenge. As regards the replacement of [Expert A], the Respondent
stated in the same email that “institutional disqualification” is appropriate to remove doubts
about concurrent conflicting interests and restore the appearance of independence and
impartiality.
27. On 29 July 2019, the Respondent in its Supplemental Brief repeated and emphasized its view
that [Arbitrator A’s] reversal of position “constitutes circumstances that give rise to justifiable
doubts about his impartiality”. It stated that it had proposed an “ethical wall” between [Expert
A] and the new expert in order to address the conflict issue because it had “learned that the
experts at [Company X] we[re] not independent contractors”. It also confirmed that it had only
“reluctantly proceeded with its formal challenge on 27 June, expecting that [Arbitrator A] would
withdraw as he had said he would”. As a result of [Arbitrator A’s] reversal, [the Respondent]
now faced a possible outcome which it had always wanted to avoid i.e. that [Arbitrator A]
would continue serving as an arbitrator after he had been formally challenged by [the
Respondent]. This would be unfair to [the Respondent] which filed its challenge with the
understanding that [Arbitrator A] would then withdraw. This “express representation” of
[Arbitrator A] so became a reason why the challenge now ought to be sustained, “regardless
of whether the challenge to [Arbitrator A] with respect to the [Expert A]-related conflict
otherwise should have been sustained”.
Decision 14 - 8

III. THE CLAIMANT’S OPPOSITION
28. The Claimant opposes the challenge and does not agree that there is a conflict requiring
[Arbitrator A’s] disqualification. [The Respondent’s] originally stated concerns - that
[Arbitrator A] might have ex parte contacts with [Expert A] in connection with the other
arbitration before or during the hearing in this arbitration and that [Arbitrator A] might be
influenced to favor [Expert A’s] opinion over that of [the Respondent’s] damages expert – are
in the Claimant’s view not sufficient to meet the LCIA’s disqualification rules and deprive [the
Claimant] of its choice of expert and the considerable investment that it has made in the work
of that expert. In this respect it finds also important that the subject matter of [Expert A’s]
report in the present arbitration is damages whereas he serves as an expert on antitrust in the
[institutional] arbitration.
29. Even so, the Claimant intended to address [the Respondent’s] concerns by advising the
Tribunal on 28 June 2019 that it had agreed to replace [Expert A] with a different expert from
[Company X]. However, it disagreed with the Claimant’s condition that the new expert be
completely “walled off” from [Expert A’s] report and team. The Claimant was surprised to note
that the Respondent’s Notice of Challenge had not even mentioned its counterproposal
(replacement of the expert but without walling off his report and his team from the new
expert).
30. As regards legal arguments, the Claimant invokes in the first place the LCIA standard as laid
down in LCIA Rule 10.1: circumstances that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s
impartiality and independence. The Claimant relies on LCIA references which have
acknowledged the role of the IBA Guidelines for the determination of the existence of
justifiable doubts.
31. The Claimant furthermore addresses the US court precedents invoked by the Respondent
which overturned arbitration decisions for a determination regarding a challenge to an
arbitrator. For the Claimant, these cases show that the standard under either the Federal
Arbitration Act or New York law is very high: the Federal Arbitration Act requires evident
partiality and New York law requires not only proof of actual bias or appearance of bias on the
part of the arbitrator, but also that the arbitrator’s (appearance of) partiality caused a prejudice
to the challenger.
32. The Claimant in its further analysis argues that “especially in light of [the Claimant’s]
replacement of [Expert A] as a damages expert with another [Company X] expert, no
circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts” about [Arbitrator A’s] impartiality and
independence because [Expert A] will not appear as an expert in this arbitration, thus mooting
the Respondent’s concerns about [Arbitrator A] meeting the expert ex parte and being biased
in favor of the expert he works with in the [institutional] arbitration. According to the Claimant,
the alleged conflict does not exist either for the mere reason that the new expert will not be
Decision 14 - 9

“walled off”: the Respondent has failed to explain how [Arbitrator A] could be biased toward a
replacement expert from [Company X], whether or not he adopts all or part of the [Expert A]
report. The Claimant quotes New York jurisprudence, according to which the likelihood of
improper influence on an arbitrator must not be speculative, but capable of demonstration,
and refers to the IBA Guidelines and LCIA References to support its view that the threshold of
“justifiable doubts” is not reached in this case. It rejects the Respondent’s suggestion that a
consulting firm should be treated in the same way as an attorney’s firm as regards their
respective relationship with an arbitrator.
33. The Claimant rejects the Respondent’s suggestion that [Expert A’s] report, materials and
supporting personnel are somehow “contaminated” and would therefore “taint” any
replacement expert and, in a second order, [Arbitrator A] himself. As any expert, the
replacement expert would come to his/her own conclusions, after considering all the evidence.
Even if that evidence includes reports, materials and analysis already generated by [Company
X], this cannot create partiality or dependence for [Arbitrator A].
34. The Claimant equally rejects in its Opposition the Respondent’s assertion that [Arbitrator A’s]
conduct in this arbitration justifies doubts about his impartiality: each of [Arbitrator A’s]
messages, in his disclosure of 13 June 2019, during the telephone conference on 25 June 2019
and in his email of 29 June 2019, were understandable and justified at the time they were
issued.
IV. THE ARBITRATOR’S COMMENTS
35. In his email of 6 July 2019, [Arbitrator A] clarified his views. He confirmed that when he learned
that [Expert A] was to act as [the Claimant’s] expert on quantum, he considered that this did
not impair his impartiality and independence, because “evaluating expert testimony on
damages is rarely a matter of the personal credibility of the expert but rather of the
persuasiveness of the expert’s analysis”. He also confirmed that thereafter, during the
telephone call of the Tribunal with the Parties, he advised the Parties that if [the Respondent]
maintained its objection to [Expert A], he would resign rather than force [the Respondent] to
pursue a challenge, because he “thought that [the Respondent] had justifiable concerns about
an arbitrator working with an expert for the other side during the pendency of the arbitration
[…], even if [he] thought that [he] would not be influenced by that”. Finally, he confirmed that,
after the possibility had been proposed that [the Claimant] might use a different expert from
[Company X], he had advised the Parties that in those circumstances he would not voluntarily
withdraw, his view being that “that the concerns that [the Respondent] might have about [his]
working with the opposing side’s expert would not apply, or would be greatly lessened, if
[Expert A] were no longer offered as expert”. He recognized that “presumably some of the
ideas in the new expert report might be derived from points made in [Expert A’s] report (which
[he had] not read and ha[d] no reason to read), but [he did] not think that arguable connection
Decision 14 - 10

is disqualifying. In this circumstance, [he] believe[d] [the Tribunal’s] obligation to keep the
arbitration moving forward and, if possible, to preserve the September hearing dates, require
that [he] continue to sit as arbitrator if [he is] able to.”
36. [Arbitrator A] further rejected the analogy of consultancy firms with law firms where conflicts
of one lawyer are imputed to the firm as a whole. In his view, there is no conflict when an
arbitrator is working with, or has worked with, a firm of the size of [Company X] or [Company
Y] (the firm of which [the Respondent’s] expert is a part, and with which [Arbitrator A] has also
worked in the past).
V. ADMISSIBILITY
37. According to Article 10.3 of the LCIA Arbitration Rules (2014) (“LCIA Rules”),
A party challenging an arbitrator under Article 10.1 shall, within 14 days of the
formation of the Arbitral Tribunal or (if later) within 14 days of becoming aware of any
grounds described in Article 10.1 or 10.2, deliver a written statement of the reasons
for its challenge to the LCIA Court, the Arbitral Tribunal and all other parties. A party
may challenge an arbitrator whom it has nominated, or in whose appointment it has
participated, only for reasons of which it becomes aware after the appointment has
been made by the LCIA Court.
38. [The Respondent] became aware of the circumstances on which it relies upon receipt of
[Arbitrator A’s] disclosure of 13 June 2019 and filed its formal challenge on 27 June 2019. The
undersigned is therefore satisfied that the challenge was submitted within the 14-day time
limit under Article 10.3 and is admissible.
39. [The Respondent] invoked other circumstances and reasons in its later submissions, however.
The “clarification” of its pending challenge which it sent to the Tribunal on 1 July 2019
contained a criticism of [Arbitrator A] which was not contained in its Notice of Challenge,
relating to the “premature statement by [Arbitrator A]” in his message of 13 June 2019 when
he “regrettably […] went further to express his view that the conflict was of no consequence”.
[The Respondent’s] message of 1 July 2019 also relied on [Arbitrator A’s] message of 29 June
2019 which in its view “embraced [the Claimant’s] position” and was part of “the way in which
this conflict has been handled by [Arbitrator A]”, allegedly demonstrating that justifiable
doubts existed about his impartiality and independence.
40. The Respondent’s Supplemental Brief dated 28 July 2019, while merely recalling “the [Expert
A]-related conflict”, concentrates on [Arbitrator A’s] alleged reversal of position which “raises
“justifiable doubts” as to his ability to perform impartially his duties as an arbitrator” (p.1) and
“constitutes circumstances that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality” (p.3).
Decision 14 - 11

41. Thus, it appears that the Respondent in its Supplemental Brief relies exclusively on
circumstances which - except for the 13 June 2019 statement of [Arbitrator A] - did not yet
exist when it filed its Notice of Challenge on 27 June 2019 and which hence cannot justify the
initial challenge. However, to the extent that [Arbitrator A’s] criticized conduct started on 13
June 2019 and spans the period before and after the Notice of Challenge and, more
importantly, could have been the subject of a separate, second notice of challenge (provided
the 14-day period requirement was fulfilled), procedural economy and the integrity of the
arbitral proceedings and their calendar (in combination with the Claimant’s failure to invoke
the inadmissibility of the additional challenge grounds of 1 July 2019 which it addressed
extensively in its Opposition of 3 July 20191) justify in the undersigned’s view to consider all
invoked grounds of challenge in this single challenge proceeding and to consider all of them
admissible.
VI. ANALYSIS OF THE CHALLENGE GROUNDS
42. The challenge is based on article 10.1 of the LCIA Rules providing that:
The LCIA Court may revoke any arbitrator’s appointment upon its own initiative, at the
written request of all other members of the Arbitral Tribunal or upon a written
challenge by any party if: (i) that arbitrator gives written notice to the LCIA Court of his
or her intent to resign as arbitrator, to be copied to all parties and all other members
of the Arbitral Tribunal (if any); (ii) that arbitrator falls seriously ill, refuses or becomes
unable or unfit to act; or (iii) circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as
to that arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
43. The third prong of this standard is applicable here, hence the concrete question to be resolved
is whether there exist circumstances that give rise to justifiable doubts about the arbitrator’s
impartiality or independence.
44. The Respondent has not indicated in its Notice of Challenge whether it considers that
[Arbitrator A’s] relationship with [Expert A] impairs [Arbitrator A’s] impartiality or his
independence or both. By referring to “[the Claimant’s] expert having parallel and
contemporaneous ex parte contact with one of the arbitrators, who would then be called upon
to judge the qualifications and credibility of that same expert”, the Respondent gives the
impression that it considers that the impartiality of the arbitrator, rather than his
independence, is at stake. The Respondent’s Supplemental Brief, which no longer addresses
the relationship as such, but concentrates on [Arbitrator A’s] conduct during the challenge
1 The Claimant did not (request leave to) react to the Supplemental Brief of the Respondent dated 29 July 2019.
Decision 14 - 12

proceedings, confirms that the Respondent’s concern is limited to the impartiality of
[Arbitrator A]:
- [Arbitrator A’s] reversal of position raises “justifiable doubts” as to his ability to perform
impartially his duties as an arbitrator”2 (p.1)
- [Arbitrator A’s] reversal constitutes circumstances that give rise to justifiable doubts as to
his impartiality3 (p.3).
45. The only occasion on which the Respondent mentioned ‘independence’ was in relation to the
independence of the replacement expert’s work (Notice of Challenge p. 4 in fine). However, if
independence was an issue in this challenge procedure, it would relate to the possible
dependence of [Arbitrator A] from [Expert A] (which the Respondent has not claimed to exist),
not the independence of the work product of the replacement expert from the initial report of
[Expert A].
46. The Respondent has not expressed a clear view on the standard which has to be applied when
determining whether circumstances exist that give rise to ‘justifiable doubts’ nor on the law
under which such standard is to be found. In its Notice of Challenge, it cited two US Supreme
Court cases which annulled an award because of the close relationship which existed between
an arbitrator and one of the parties. In its Supplemental Brief it has not mentioned any further
precedents.
47. The Claimant addressed the possibly relevant legal standards and authorities in more detail
and relied in its Opposition on both the LCIA standard and the New York and Federal standards.
The Respondent has not objected to these standards in its Supplemental Brief which remained
silent on the applicable standards.
48. The undersigned is of the view that, this arbitration being organized under the LCIA Rules, it is
justified and required, when determining whether “justifiable doubts” as envisaged by Article
10.1 of the LCIA Rules exist, to take into account what the LCIA Court has held in other cases
where the term had to be applied. However, the relevance of the determinations made in other
LCIA References may be limited by the arbitration law which was applicable in those cases and
which may have influenced the determination. Therefore, the US law authorities which have
been cited by the Parties will also be taken into account as the term “justifiable doubts” has to
be interpreted also in accordance with the applicable arbitration law.
49. In the first case relied on by the Respondent - exclusively - in support of its argument that the
degree of impartiality required of an arbitrator is the same as that of a judge, Commonwealth
Coatings Corp. v. Continental Cas. Co. (393 U.S. 145 (1968)), the US Supreme Court held that

“any tribunal permitted by law to try cases and controversies not only must be unbiased but
also must avoid even the appearance of bias” (plurality of four Justices) and vacated an award
rendered by a tribunal comprising an arbitrator who had failed to disclose a close and long-
standing financial relationship with one of the parties. However, the failure to disclose was
rejected as a ground for vacation of the award by the minority, which did “not believe that it is
either necessary, appropriate, or permissible to rule, as the Court does, that, regardless of the
facts, innocent failure to volunteer information constitutes the ‘evident partiality’ necessary
under s 10(b) of the Arbitration Act to set aside an award. ‘Evident partiality’ means what it
says: conduct - or at least an attitude or disposition - by the arbitrator favoring one party rather
than the other”. The standard to be deducted from this case is thus not clear, “evident
partiality” as provided in the Federal Arbitration Act being a higher (and more objective)
standard than the one adopted by the majority for which the mere appearance of bias has to
be avoided. It even remains uncertain whether it is sufficient that this “appearance” exists in
the challenging party’s mind or must be more objective.
50. The second case referred to by the Respondent, Matter of Shomron v Fuks4, served to support
its view that it is more appropriate to remove the new counsel (or, in the present case, the
expert who appears in the case) rather than the arbitrator who has been involved longer and
deeper in the case. The Supreme Court decided to reinstate the arbitrator who had been
disqualified by the AAA and to disqualify instead the counsel who by his sudden appearance in
the case as fourth counsel of the respondent had created the conflict with the arbitrator. The
Court did not expand on the standard of impartiality, however, and merely referred (implicitly
approving) to the AAA’s and the Court of Appeal’s finding that there was an “appearance of
partiality”.
51. In short, the US authorities relied upon by the Respondent are not helpful to determine the
test for the “justifiable doubts” as meant in Article 10.1 of the LCIA Rules.
52. The Claimant in its Opposition referred to a decision of the US Court of Appeals, Second Circuit
which found that after the above mentioned Supreme Court’s Commonwealth Coatings
decision “we are left in the dark as to whether an ‘appearance of bias’ will suffice to meet the
seemingly more stringent ‘evident partiality’ standard of 9 U.S.C. § 10”. Hence the Court of
Appeals examined prior decisions of the same circuit and, after finding that “the standard of
‘appearance of bias’ is too low for the invocation of Section 10 and ‘proof of actual bias’ too
high”, held that “ ‘evident partiality’ within the meaning of USC §10 will be found where a
reasonable person would have to conclude that an arbitrator was partial to one party to the
arbitration” (Morelite Const. Corp. v. New York Dist. Council Carpenters Ben. Funds, 748 F.2d
79, 84 (2d Cir. 1984).

53. The Claimant also referred to New York law and court cases applying CPLR § 7511, according
to which
- “an award may be vacated only if (1) the rights of a party were prejudiced by corruption,
fraud or misconduct in procuring the award, or by the partiality of the arbitrator;” and
holding that the burden of proof of the petitioner under this clause “requires clear and
convincing evidence, that any impropriety on the part of the arbitrator prejudiced the
petitioner's rights or the integrity of the arbitration process” (Piller v. Eisner, No.2017-
08968, 2019 WL 2518696, at 2).
- “The type of relationship that would appear to disqualify an arbitrator and should
therefore be disclosed is one from which it may not be unreasonable to infer an absence
of impartiality, the presence of bias or the existence of some interest on the part of the
arbitrator in the welfare of one of the parties” (Burden v. Erie Ins. Co., 64 Misc. 3d 1201
(A) (N.Y.Sup.Ct.2019).
54. Having duly considered these authorities and the others mentioned by the Claimant, the
undersigned comes to the conclusion that US federal and New York state law as applied by the
courts in order to grant vacatur of an award require that the appearance of bias be
“reasonable”, which in the undersigned’s view includes an element of objectivity, similar to
that of the LCIA standard on which the Claimant has equally relied. It is noted that the US
standard is drawn from cases relating to possible vacation of an arbitral award by a court.
Neither Party provided US authorities on the standard to be applied by arbitral institutions
deciding on challenges or reasons why the standard to be applied by such bodies should be
different from those applied by the courts. The undersigned is therefore confident that the
circumstances of the present challenge have to be assessed “reasonably”, i.e. through the eyes
of a reasonable third person, under US law, and that this standard aligns well with the LCIA
standard.
55. By referring to “justifiable doubts”, the LCIA Rules impose an objective approach which
requires considering the point of view of a reasonable, informed and fair-minded third party
(LCIA Reference No. 1462683 at § 239). It is noted that that Reference, on which the Claimant
also relies, concerned an arbitration with seat in London and applicable English law and applied
the test established by English case law: “whether the fair-minded and informed observer,
having considered the facts, would conclude that there is a real possibility that an arbitrator is
partial to a party” (Magill v. Porter, [2001] UKHL, 67, para 103). The undersigned is confident
that this test will lead to the same result as the US “reasonableness” test.
56. Even if the above tests developed in US federal law, New York state law and English law all
relate to impartiality, the undersigned considers them applicable in the present challenge,
even if Article 10.1 of the LCIA Rules which the Respondent relied upon refers to both
impartiality and independence. Indeed, as indicated in para. 44 above, it is justified to
understand the Respondent’s submissions as concerning possible partiality, rather than
possible dependence.
Decision 14 - 15

57. The Claimant pointed out that the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in International
Arbitration (“IBA Guidelines”) which are frequently cited in the LCIA References deciding
challenges to arbitrators, consider disqualification of an arbitrator appropriate “if facts or
circumstances exist, or have arisen since the appointment, which, from the point of view of a
reasonable third person having knowledge of the relevant facts and circumstances, would give
rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality or independence”, and that the IBA
Guidelines can thus be particularly relevant to determine when doubts are justifiable (cfr. LCIA
Reference No.132551 at Summary §§ 116-117 and LCIA Reference No. UN101693 at §§ 14-15).
58. The undersigned thus concludes that for this challenge to succeed, the Respondent’s concerns
must be objectively reasonable, i.e. justified in the eyes of a fair-minded third person. When
ascertaining whether the Respondent’s apprehension or fear of bias is reasonable, all relevant
facts and circumstances shall be considered.
59. The Respondent has invoked several “circumstances” and reasons, with a different emphasis
on some of them as time went by. Initially, the circumstance which created the Respondent’s
concern and which apparently prompted the challenge consisted in the relationship of
[Arbitrator A] with the Claimant’s quantum expert. In later comments, the Respondent has
relied more on the allegedly inappropriate conduct of [Arbitrator A] since his disclosure. Since
the purpose of the challenge procedure is to safeguard the integrity of the arbitration
proceedings, both the initial grounds for the challenge and the subsequent conduct of
[Arbitrator A] will be analyzed hereafter.
60. As a preliminary matter, it must be emphasized that it is undisputed between the Parties that
both the Claimant and [Arbitrator A] had no hand in the alleged conflict as it arose and that

simultaneously as expert for a party represented by [Arbitrator A’s] firm in the [institutional]

having previously worked on the [institutional] matter with another partner of [Arbitrator A’s]
firm, [Partner M], and his team. It is thus established that neither the Claimant, nor [Arbitrator
A] have been negligent and that neither could have discovered the alleged conflict earlier than
they did.
61. It is also correct that [the Respondent] did not cause the conflict, as [Lawyer Q of Law Firm B]
put it in his email of 1 July 2019 to the Tribunal and the LCIA.

- after his engagement by [Arbitrator A’s] firm for the [institutional] arbitration, toward the
end of April 2019, [Expert A] worked with [Partner M] and his team;
- [Expert A] met [Arbitrator A] first at the end of May 2019 and they spoke on the phone “a
couple of times”, but [Expert A] is “largely working with other members of the firm”;
- [Expert A] expert report in the [institutional] arbitration is due in early September 2019,
around the same time as the scheduled hearing dates in the LCIA arbitration;
- [Expert A’s] expert report in the [institutional] arbitration will bear on [licensing] and

[the Claimant’s] expert having parallel and contemporaneous ex parte contact with one of the
arbitrators, who then would be called upon to judge the qualifications and credibility of that
same expert at the hearing”.
64. The undersigned agrees that the contemporaneous parallel contacts of an arbitrator with one
of the parties’ experts may give rise to doubts which are reasonable and that even the prospect
of such contacts is sufficient to justly alert the other party. However, the above facts show that
[Arbitrator A] did neither chose nor engage [Expert A] as an expert and that he has not even
substantially worked with him in the [institutional] arbitration. There is thus no reason to
assume that the limited professional contact which existed before the disclosure has in some
way impacted on [Arbitrator A’s] impartiality or independence in the present arbitration. The
limited scope of this purely professional contact also explains and justifies [Arbitrator A’s]
declaration of 13 June 2019 that it did not impair his impartiality or independence.
65. It is in this connection relevant that [Arbitrator A] did not himself choose [Expert A] to act as
an expert for the [institutional] arbitration. Had this been the case, this choice could have been

an indication of prior acquaintance or experience of [Arbitrator A] with [Expert A] and of

would not amount to partiality in favour of [Expert A], this hypothesis is in any event denied

and the few telephone calls between [Expert A] and [Arbitrator A] are clearly not of the kind

member of the larger team of his firm working in the [institutional] arbitration) were to work

In the case of experts appearing before an arbitral tribunal or a court, however, the expert
presents and, if needed, defends his personal professional views. In this respect, which is the
only one relevant for our purposes, he is independent. The undersigned agrees with the
Claimant that “any expert will come to his or her own conclusions, as every expert is expected
to do, after considering all of the relevant evidence” (Opposition p. 15).

his/her team not access the [Expert A] report, including tabs 4, 5, 6, and 8, or communicate

impartiality.”

“the expert disqualification standard must be distinguished from the attorney-client
relationship because experts perform very different functions in litigation than attorneys”
which seems right to the undersigned. Nor has the Respondent contradicted the distinction

“Imputation of conflicts in law firms are driven by concerns about (a) protecting a
client’s confidential information, (b) ensuring zealous advocacy by the law firm
(which might be impaired if the lawyer is working adverse to a client of the law firm),
and (c) a policy judgment about a lawyer’s fiduciary obligations to his or her client (a

where an expert for a party is working with an arbitrator in another matter. In those

connection with, in this case, the fairly large firm of which the expert is a part.”

91. The undersigned understands that, even if Article 10.7 of the LCIA Rules authorizes the LCIA
Court to refer all or part of the costs to a later decision of the Tribunal, the LCIA Court’s present
policy is not to do so but to determine itself such costs and their allocation, presumably in an
effort to discourage unmeritorious challenges.
92. The present case may justify that the LCIA Court defer the decision to the Tribunal, however.
In the first place, because the Claimant’s letter of 30 July 2019 reports costs in an amount of
USD 89,861.40 without substantiating them and without the Respondent having had the
opportunity to comment on that amount. As the challenge is rejected and no replacement
arbitrator is to be appointed, the upcoming hearing date of 4 - 13 September 2019 can still be
kept if the challenge decision is issued without further delay. The undersigned therefore
prefers to defer the decision (and whatever preceding submissions on costs may still be
required) to the Tribunal.
93. A second reason to defer the decision is the particular nature of this challenge which was
initially based on a conflict between an arbitrator and an expert but which could be timely
solved by the agreed replacement of the expert, the sole disagreement being about the level
of screening required of the replacement expert (as stated by the Respondent itself on p.4 of
its Supplemental Brief dated 28 July 2019). The Tribunal, which has previously participated in
the exchange with the Parties about the replacement of the expert and which will eventually
be assessing the expert testimony, will have a more complete view of elements which may
influence the allocation of costs.
VIII. DECISION
1. The challenge is admissible.
2. The challenge is rejected.
3. The costs relating to the challenge shall be determined and allocated by the Tribunal
in its final or, if it deems appropriate, in another decision.
